newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGBs end firmer in slow trade before key events.
newsitem.headline: JGBs end firmer in slow trade before key events.

text.p: Key September 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) futures closed a quiet session slightly firmer on Monday ahead of key events set for later this week, including Tuesday's 10-year JGB auction.
The other events are the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) release of its quarterly tankan corporate survey on Wednesday and May industrial output data due out on Friday, traders said.

After initial selling on the yen's fall against the dollar, short-covering emerged from those who had gone short before the weekend meeting of Group of Seven (G7) leaders, and this provided a solid floor for the rest of the day, they said.
The September ended up 0.04 at 123.91 on turnover of 18,342 contracts. The contract moved between 123.79 and 124.06 after opening at 123.81.

"The dollar's gains triggered selling in JGBs in the morning. But given the G7 statement (in which Japan promises to expand domestic demand), a change in the BOJ's monetary policy is unlikely in the near future, and this view provided firm support for JGBs," said a long-term credit bank dealer.
The G7 economic statement said that Japan has the objective of achieving strong domestic demand-led growth and avoiding a significant increase in its external surplus.
Although comments about Japan's trade surplus emerged at the summit, they were basically as expected by the market and held no surprises, traders said.

U.S. President Bill Clinton warned Japan that a return to "exploding" trade surpluses with the United States would hurt both countries. He added that the decision by the Japanese government to try to pursue a path of fiscal austerity ran the risk of going back to an old export-driven strategy of growth.
But the overall mildness of the comments over Japan's trade surplus helped the dollar to firm. It rose as high as 115.67 yen, against 114.80/90 yen at Friday's New York close.
"Trade was thin ahead of the auction tomorrow, although nobody so far has shown strong interest in the new issue," said a dealer at a long-term credit bank's securities unit.

It will be the first auction from which both Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd and Nomura Securities Co Ltd are suspended. Traders said a slight hope for brokers is that if the new bond's coupon is set at 2.6 percent, which is highly likely, MOF could reopen the 2.6 percent 193rd 10-year issue, and it could become the new benchmark later this year. The MOF announces terms for the new bond at 8.30 a.m. on Tuesday (2330 GMT Monday).

"The market has been a bit too pessimistic about the tankan recently. That means if the tankan shows a great improvement, the contract could fall more than one yen to 122.50," said the second dealer. A Reuters poll of economists showed they expect the diffusion index for major manufacturers to range from minus four to plus four, against plus two in the March tankan.
Some traders said today's rise to 124.06 filled in a gap the September made last week between Thursday's closing at 124.06 and Friday's opening at 123.76.
Cash bond activity was slim, with key 182nd 10-year JGB yielding down 0.005 at 2.390 percent at 0653 GMT.
